Phase 10: Multi-City Expansion
Controlled City Replication, Operations and Phase 11 Gate
Executive decision
Approve Phase 10 with one major condition: launch the two new cities sequentially—
not simultaneously.
Recommended six-month sequence:
Proven City
↓
City 2: controlled cluster launch
↓
City 2 reaches stability gate
↓
City 3: controlled cluster launch
↓
Network operating system validated

The strategic objective is not to display more city names on the website. It is to prove that
the complete marketplace system can be reproduced in another geography:
• Demand acquisition
• Sitter recruitment
• Partner verification
• Scheduling
• Subscription fulfilment
• Society partnerships
• Payments and payouts
• Incident response
• Customer support
• Positive city-level contribution
India’s broader pet-care market is expanding rapidly, but market growth does not remove
fulfilment risk. IBEF estimated the wider Indian pet-care industry at approximately ₹30,434
crore in CY2024, while projecting substantial growth through 2032. This makes expansion
attractive, but operational reliability—not market size—will determine whether a multi-city
service marketplace survives.
1. Phase 10 principle
Wrong expansion model
Launch six cities
↓
Recruit large numbers of applicants
↓
Run ads everywhere
↓
Accept bookings before local density exists
↓
Partners travel long distances
↓

Bookings fail
↓
Support and refunds increase
↓
Brand trust declines nationally
Correct expansion model
Select one city
↓
Select two or three micro-markets
↓
Validate demand before public launch
↓
Build verified local supply
↓
Run a closed beta
↓
Reach quality and contribution gates
↓
Expand inside the city
↓
Replicate in the next city
The actual expansion unit is not a city.
The expansion unit is a dense service cluster containing customers, societies, sitters,
backup supply and local support.
Examples:
• Bengaluru → HSR–Koramangala
• Pune → Baner–Balewadi
• Mumbai → Powai–Chandivali
• Gurugram → Golf Course Road societies

• Ahmedabad → Thaltej–Bodakdev
• Surat → Vesu–VIP Road

• One existing mature city

6. Why cluster operations are mandatory
Indian metro traffic creates substantial fulfilment risk. TomTom’s 2025 India index reported
Bengaluru at a 74.4% average congestion level, with Pune and Mumbai also among the
country’s most congested operating environments. This makes city-wide sitter pools,
cross-city assignments and broad exact-time guarantees operationally unsafe.

City

A sitter should normally operate within one cluster during a service block.
Cluster launch criteria
Each launch cluster should have:
• 300–1,500 addressable pet households
• Three or more target societies or dense neighbourhood zones
• Five to ten active sitters or walkers
• Two or more backup sitters

• Local grooming/training partners where those services are live
• One veterinary referral network
• One operations owner
• Maximum travel-time rules
• Local service pricing
• Capacity limits by time window

Gig and platform workers
The Code on Social Security defines platform work, and a June 2026 Labour Ministry
communication states that the Social Security Rules, 2026 require aggregators to share
details of gig and platform workers electronically. A pet-care marketplace should obtain a
formal opinion on whether it is an in-scope aggregator and implement eShram
onboarding/reporting where applicable.
Privacy
The notified DPDP Rules, 2025 have phased commencement. Multi-city expansion
increases the number of employees and partners accessing addresses, recurring
schedules, pet-care instructions and health-related records, so role-based access, city-
level permissions, processing notices and audit trails should be operational before
expansion.
Consumer support
India’s E-Commerce Rules require consumer-facing grievance mechanisms. New cities
must not launch until customers have a visible escalation channel and central support
knows which local team owns each case.

GST and marketplace settlement
Where the platform collects customer consideration for supplies made through third-party
providers, e-commerce-operator and TCS treatment depends on the actual transaction
structure. Maintain city-, partner- and service-level ledgers and obtain a written tax position
before expanding settlement flows across states.

Executive decision
Your principle is correct:

However, the proposed readiness table contains several internal inconsistencies. The

• 100 active walking subscribers receiving 12–20 walks each would generate

5. Current city-operating signals
Ahmedabad
Ahmedabad’s 2025 average congestion level was 49%, lower than Bengaluru, Pune,
Mumbai, Hyderabad, Chennai and Jaipur in TomTom’s current city data. That does not
eliminate travel problems, but it can make controlled route operations more manageable.
Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation also operates an official pet-dog registration system.

Existing dog-walking subscriptions are already publicly advertised in Ahmedabad, so the
category is not completely undeveloped; differentiation must come from local trust, better
reliability and society integration.
Best role: controlled first city or regional operating base.
Bengaluru
Bengaluru offers strong subscription-validation potential, but it is operationally difficult.
TomTom recorded a 74.4% average congestion level in 2025 and approximately 36 minutes
for a 10 km drive. Existing providers already market monthly, GPS-tracked walking
subscriptions, demonstrating both customer familiarity and active competition.
Best role: strongest digital product-market-fit test, but only through micro-market clusters.
Pune
Pune recorded 71.1% average congestion in 2025, so cross-city sitter assignment would be
risky. Current providers also advertise subscription-based walking, meaning value,
continuity and society density—not merely subscription availability—must differentiate the
offer.
Best role: balanced second metro and strong society/subscription market.
Hyderabad
Hyderabad had a 55.5% average congestion level in 2025—still significant, but lower than
Bengaluru, Pune and Mumbai. Existing providers advertise daily monthly walking
subscriptions there, indicating that the recurring-care category already has market
visibility.
Best role: should move earlier in a metro-first sequence than your original order suggests.
Gurugram
Current providers advertise monthly walking subscriptions in Gurugram. Its strongest
strategic fit is not merely walking volume, but premium society contracts, verified partner
pools and corporate-adjacent demand.
Best role: premium society and B2B validation city.
Mumbai

Mumbai offers high-value convenience potential, but TomTom recorded a 63.2% average
congestion level in 2025. Subscription competitors are already present, making tight
service radii and locality-level supply essential.
Best role: later premium launch after route-density and backup systems are mature.
Chennai
Walking services are currently marketed in Chennai, and Greater Chennai Corporation
operates an official pet-licensing system; it reported issuing 9,115 pet-animal licences
during 2024. Chennai also recorded 58.6% average congestion in 2025.
Best role: attractive later metro, requiring local-language operations, city-specific
licensing guidance and cluster planning.
Delhi NCR deeper expansion
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi operates an official annual pet-dog registration process
tied to vaccination validity. This reinforces the need for city-specific documentation and
resident guidance when expanding beyond Gurugram into Delhi’s municipal jurisdictions.
Best role: expand after Gurugram rather than treating all NCR jurisdictions as one
operating city.

Phase 10 City Launch Gate System
End-to-End Validation, Supply Build, Soft Launch and City-Scale Playbook
Executive verdict
Approve the gated city-launch model, but strengthen it before using it operationally.
Your four gates are directionally correct, but the current version has three weaknesses:
1. It measures too many vanity inputs—waitlist sign-ups and sitter applications—
without proving that they will convert into paying demand and active supply.
2. The proposed launch-quality thresholds are too weak. A 90% completion rate and
5–10% sitter no-show rate are not acceptable for a trust-sensitive pet-care
marketplace.
3. It omits explicit gates for economics, safety, compliance, privacy and launch
capacity.
The corrected sequence should be:
Gate 0: City selection and compliance
↓
Gate 1: Qualified demand
↓

Gate 2: Active supply and backup capacity
↓
Gate 3: Operational readiness
↓
Gate 4: Closed-beta quality
↓
Gate 5: Cluster economics and repeat demand
↓
Gate 6: Public city expansion
The operating rule is:
A city is not launched because its landing page is live. It is launched only when
customers can book, providers can fulfil, support can intervene, incidents can be
managed and the city can generate positive contribution.
1. How the gate system should work
Gates must be sequential and blocking.
A city cannot compensate for weak supply with strong demand. It cannot compensate for
poor service quality with high revenue. It cannot compensate for positive economics with
unresolved safety incidents.
Each gate should produce one of three decisions:
Decision Meaning
Pass All critical thresholds met; proceed
Conditional pass Minor gaps exist with a dated corrective plan
Fail/Hold Do not proceed; repair the failed gate
Critical gate rule
The following cannot receive a conditional pass:
• No accountable local operator
• No emergency escalation process
• No usable backup provider pool

• Critical safety incident unresolved
• Payment or refund process not working
• Customer support unavailable
• Required local compliance not assessed
• Negative contribution with no credible correction
• Serious privacy or access-control weakness

adequate grievance mechanism. Deposit, refund and cancellation terms should therefore
be shown before payment.

Your city operating model is directionally correct, but it should be organised by city
maturity, not copied as a fixed seven-person team into every new market.
The recommended operating principle is:

Start with one accountable city leader and a small cross-functional launch pod. Add

• Qualified demand

• Backup coverage
• Local operational ownership
• Emergency escalation
• Positive projected unit economics
• Capacity for the services being advertised

19. Why travel-time clusters matter
TomTom’s 2025 data reports average congestion of approximately 74.4% for Bengaluru and
49% for Ahmedabad. Bengaluru therefore requires tighter operating radii and stronger
peak-time capacity controls than Ahmedabad.
This is an operational inference:
• An Ahmedabad cluster may sometimes cover several adjacent residential areas.
• A Bengaluru cluster that appears close on a map may still be unworkable during
morning and evening peaks.
• Walker routes should be defined using measured service-to-service travel times.

15. Index strategy
Typical high-value indexes include:
CREATE INDEX bookings_city_status_time_idx

ON bookings (city_id, status, scheduled_at);
CREATE INDEX bookings_zone_date_idx
ON bookings (service_zone_id, scheduled_at);
CREATE INDEX partner_service_area_geo_idx
ON partner_service_areas
USING GIST (origin);
CREATE INDEX active_price_items_idx
ON price_book_items (price_book_id, service_package_id)
WHERE is_active = true;
PostgreSQL supports multicolumn indexes and partial indexes, but the column order and
predicate should match real query patterns. Indexes improve reads while adding write and
maintenance overhead, so they should be driven by observed workloads.
Use pg_stat_statements to identify expensive and frequent queries rather than guessing
every index in advance.
16. Table partitioning
Do not create one physical bookings table per city.
Begin with a shared bookings table containing:
city_id
service_zone_id
scheduled_at
When the volume justifies partitioning, append-heavy tables are generally better
partitioned by time, such as month, rather than by a growing and uneven set of cities.
Good partition candidates:
• Bookings
• Notification events
• Audit logs
• Payment events
• Capacity snapshots
• Location events

PostgreSQL supports declarative partitioning and partition pruning; however, partitioning
adds operational complexity and should be introduced only when row volume and query
behaviour justify it.

Phase 10 Multi-City Brand Strategy
One National Brand, Six Local Market Playbooks
Executive verdict
Approve the national-master-brand model with city-specific positioning.
Do not create six independent brands. That would fragment:
• Trust and reviews
• Verification standards
• Product development
• Support systems
• Search authority

• Safety reputation
• Marketing expenditure
Use one national promise:
Verified local pet care, documented at every visit.
Then localise five elements for each city:
1. Customer problem
2. Flagship product
3. Operational service area
4. Pricing and offer
5. Local trust evidence
India’s pet-care category continues to expand as pets are increasingly treated as family
members and spending shifts toward professional services, digital discovery and premium
care. However, national category growth does not prove that the same positioning or price
will work in every neighbourhood.
1. National brand architecture
Recommended brand core
Your proposed core is:
Verified pet care with trusted sitters, live updates, report cards and emergency support.
A safer and stronger version is:
Verified local pet care with trusted caregivers, live service updates, detailed care
reports and urgent-care coordination.
Why change “emergency support”?
“Emergency support” can sound like the platform provides veterinary treatment.
Your platform should promise:
• Emergency clinic information
• Human coordination
• Record-sharing assistance
• Transport coordination where available
• Customer escalation

It should not promise:
• Diagnosis
• Treatment
• Guaranteed clinic admission
• Guaranteed veterinary response time
• Medical prioritisation for paid members
Use:
Urgent-care coordination
rather than:
Emergency medical support
2. Four national brand pillars
Pillar 1: Verified people
Every provider profile should show exactly what was verified.
Valid badges
• Identity checked
• Contact verified
• Documents reviewed
• Practical trial completed
• Dog-walking skills assessed
• Cat-care skills assessed
• Society access approved
• Background check completed on [date]
Avoid vague badges
• 100% safe
• Government approved
• Fully certified
• Police verified
• Best sitter

unless the claim is literally true, current and documented.
A “police verification” badge should appear only when the relevant check was actually
completed, with the type and date visible. It must not imply government endorsement or
guarantee that the provider presents no risk.
Pillar 2: Visible service
The customer should be able to see that the promised care happened.
National service-proof standard
• Start check-in
• End check-out
• GPS route where appropriate
• Time and duration
• Photo or media proof with consent
• Toilet and behaviour notes
• Food, water or medication confirmation
• Incident flag
• Digital report card
GPS tracking and live updates are already promoted by existing Indian dog-walking
services. In competitive metros, these are becoming expected product features rather than
sufficient premium differentiators.
Your differentiation must therefore combine tracking with:
• Better caregiver continuity
• Better backup fulfilment
• Better reports
• Faster problem resolution
• Stronger society protocols
Pillar 3: Reliable continuity
Use:
Preferred caregiver with approved backup coverage

Do not use:
Guaranteed same sitter forever
Recommended service targets:
Metric Target
Preferred-caregiver fulfilment 85%+
Primary or approved backup fulfilment 98%+
Unintroduced replacement Below 2%
Provider no-show Below 1%
The brand promise should be continuity with resilience—not dependence on one person.
Pillar 4: Local readiness
A city page should never imply city-wide coverage when only one cluster is operational.
Every local page must show:
• Exact active neighbourhoods
• Services currently available
• Current operating hours
• Starting prices
• Verified local provider count
• Backup coverage where applicable
• Local support contact
• Local urgent-care directory
• Waitlist for unsupported areas
This prevents national marketing from outrunning actual city operations.

Part III — Company-Owned vs Franchise Expansion
9. Company-owned cities
Advantages
• Direct control over verification
• Consistent safety processes
• Better training
• Centralised customer experience
• Reliable data
• Easier pricing control
• Direct city P&L visibility
• Faster intervention after incidents
Disadvantages
• Higher capital requirements
• Slower geographic expansion
• Greater recruitment burden
• Higher central-management complexity
• Greater fixed-cost exposure
Best use
Company-owned operations should be used for:
• The first three to five cities
• Major brand-defining metros

• Cities containing new service experiments
• Markets with complex routing or high expectations
• Cities used to train future regional operators
Recommendation
Keep these company-owned initially:
• First/core city
• Bengaluru
• Pune
• Mumbai
• Gurugram
• Ahmedabad, if it is the core operating base
The exact list should follow the actual expansion sequence rather than an arbitrary
population ranking.
10. Traditional franchise cities
Advantages
• Lower central capital requirement
• Faster local hiring
• Local relationship advantage
• Local society access
• Faster geographic coverage
Risks
• Provider-verification shortcuts
• Different refund practices
• Hidden incidents
• Inconsistent training
• Poor payment discipline
• Unauthorised pricing
• Customer-data leakage

• Weak sitter payouts
• Brand damage spreading nationally
A franchise arrangement in India requires a carefully drafted commercial contract and
authorised trademark use. Franchise disputes are expressly recognised among
commercial disputes, while the underlying relationship also involves ordinary contract and
trademark law.
Franchise operation does not remove the need for consumer grievance handling, fair e-
commerce conduct or transparent cancellation and refund rules.
11. Recommended hybrid: Managed City Operator
Before offering a conventional franchise, use a more controlled model:
Managed City Operating Partner

• Brand

• Verification standards

• Quality auditing
Local operating partner owns
• Field recruitment
• Practical trials under central standards

• Local availability management
• Society outreach
• Local events

• Daily schedule coordination
• Local service recovery
• Local team management
Central company must retain step-in rights
The central team must be able to:
• Pause a city
• Pause a service
• Suspend a provider
• Take over customer support
• Freeze acquisition
• Audit customer and provider records
• Replace the operator
• Terminate brand access
12. What a franchise or operating partner must never control alone
Do not delegate final authority over:
• Critical-incident classification
• Deletion of complaints or reviews
• Provider identity verification
• Safety-policy exceptions
• Customer refunds
• Customer funds
• Partner-payout records
• Medical claims
• Customer-data exports

• Subscription-credit adjustments
• City-quality reporting
The DPDP Rules, 2025 have phased commencement, but a multi-operator model should
already use purpose-specific notices, role-based access, security safeguards and
grievance handling.
Platform-worker and aggregator obligations must also be assessed consistently across
company-owned and operator-managed cities. The Code on Social Security recognises gig
and platform workers, and 2026 central-rule developments reinforce the need for worker
registration, engagement and reporting systems.

14. Recommended franchise economics
Avoid rewarding an operator on total customer GMV.
An operator should be rewarded for:
• Completed services
• Positive city contribution

• Quality
• Society conversion
• Provider reliability
Better compensation model
Fixed local management fee
+
Performance share of city contribution
+
Quality and growth bonus
Illustrative structure:
• Small fixed operating fee
• 20–35% share of contribution after direct city costs
• Bonus for quality, repeat rate and society renewals
• No share on refunded or disputed transactions
• Penalties for concealed incidents or payout failures
This is strategically safer than giving a local operator a large percentage of GMV regardless
of service quality.

role-scoped access and auditable grievance handling for addresses, schedules, pet

5. Important GPS-tracking rule
Do not track sitters continuously
The correct location model is:
Sitter accepts booking
↓
Sitter travels toward service area
↓
Sitter explicitly starts service
↓
Tracking session begins
↓
Walk or visit is completed
↓
Tracking session stops
↓
Route/report saved
Avoid:
Sitter installs app
↓
Platform tracks location all day
Recommended location states

LOCATION_OFF
PRE_SERVICE_OPTIONAL
ACTIVE_SERVICE_TRACKING
PAUSED
SERVICE_COMPLETED
LOCATION_UPLOAD_PENDING
Permission design
Request location only when the sitter activates the relevant feature.
Apple requires location use to be directly relevant to the app’s function and requires notice
and consent before location data is collected or used. Apple also advises developers to
use background updates only when real-time background information is genuinely needed.
On Android, background location requires a separate permission model; on Android 11 and
later, users generally enable “Allow all the time” from system settings. Google Play permits
background location only when it is important to the app’s core functionality and requires a
declaration, prominent disclosure, privacy policy and review evidence.
Best implementation
Use background location only for an active, user-started walk session.
This produces a defensible core use case:
Tracking the pet’s service route while the sitter performs the booked walk, including when
the screen is locked.
Do not use location for:
• Advertising
• General sitter monitoring
• Attendance outside booked services
• Unrelated analytics
• Persistent employee surveillance
Battery and accuracy
Background location can materially affect battery life, and Android may throttle
background updates. Use:
• Moderate update intervals
• Distance-based updates

• Automatic timeouts
• Immediate stop after service completion
• Upload batching
• Location-quality indicators
• Offline storage with later synchronisation
Android’s official guidance recommends removing updates when no longer needed and
setting reasonable timeouts to prevent continued battery consumption.

12. Wallet versus service credits
Use the word credits rather than “wallet” in the initial release.
Recommended design:
• Non-transferable
• No cash withdrawal
• No peer-to-peer transfer
• Used only for eligible platform bookings
• Issued for subscription entitlement, refund, promotion or service recovery
• Separate balances by credit type
• Full transaction history
RBI distinguishes closed-system instruments used only to buy the issuer’s own goods or
services from broader prepaid payment instruments. Because your marketplace may
facilitate third-party service providers, a reloadable customer-funded balance can create
additional regulatory questions. Obtain payments counsel before creating cash-like stored
value, transferability or third-party merchant acceptance.
Recommended Phase 11 approach
Launch:
• Subscription service credits
• Promotional credits
• Refund credits with customer choice where lawful

• Loyalty credits
Defer:
• User-funded cash wallet
• Peer transfer
• Cash-out
• Cross-merchant usage
• Stored balances unrelated to an active service obligation

17. Cross-platform versus native
Cross-platform is appropriate when
• The team is strong in TypeScript/Dart

• Most features share common UI and logic
• Faster simultaneous iOS/Android delivery matters
• Native bridges for GPS, camera, push and background jobs are tested carefully
Fully native may be justified when
• Background location is highly complex
• Device-level performance is critical
• The team already has strong iOS and Android specialists
• Platform-specific workflows differ significantly
• Reliability outweighs initial development speed
Practical recommendation
Use a well-supported cross-platform framework for both apps, but treat these as native-
critical modules:
• Location
• Background service/session
• Push
• Camera and uploads
• Secure storage
• Biometrics
• Offline database
• Deep links
Do not choose the framework solely from developer familiarity. Run a technical proof of
concept for:
1. Screen locked during a 45-minute walk
2. Location retained with expected battery use
3. Network lost and restored
4. Photo/report upload retry
5. Push received across device states
6. App killed and reopened
7. Permission denied and later enabled

12. React Native with Expo vs Flutter
Option A: React Native with Expo
Advantages for your context
• TypeScript and React knowledge transfers directly
• Easier alignment with a Next.js team
• Shared domain types and API clients
• Faster hiring from JavaScript/React talent pools
• Expo provides an integrated framework and native-device APIs
• Native modules can still be added where required
React Native’s own setup documentation recommends using a framework for new
applications, and Expo provides a React Native framework with routing, build tooling and
native-device modules.
Risks

• Background-location behaviour still varies by operating system
• Some native libraries require development builds or custom configuration
• Poorly selected third-party packages can cause upgrade friction
• JavaScript knowledge does not remove the need to understand iOS and Android
lifecycle behaviour
Expo’s current tooling supports React Native’s newer architecture, but third-party-library
compatibility should still be checked before adoption.
Option B: Flutter
Advantages
• Strong UI consistency
• Highly controlled rendering
• Single Dart codebase
• Mature architecture guidance
• Excellent for custom interfaces and motion-heavy applications
Flutter officially positions itself as a framework for natively compiled multiplatform
applications from one codebase and publishes detailed scalable-app architecture
guidance.
Costs for your context
• Requires Dart expertise
• Less direct code and knowledge reuse from Next.js/React
• Separate frontend hiring profile
• Shared TypeScript domain packages cannot be consumed directly
• Web and mobile teams may diverge more quickly
Final framework decision
Use React Native with Expo when:
• Your existing stack is React/Next.js
• Your team is strongest in TypeScript
• Speed and shared engineering practices matter

• You are prepared to test native-critical modules thoroughly
Use Flutter when:
• You have a dedicated Flutter team
• Visual consistency is the dominant requirement
• You accept a separate language and mobile architecture
• You are not optimising for React/TypeScript reuse
For your current full-stack profile, React Native with Expo is the stronger default.

11. GPS session architecture
Session-based tracking only

↓

↓

↓

↓

Do not track sitters continuously throughout the working day.
Apple permits background services only for their intended purposes and requires location
use to be directly relevant to app functionality. Android requires appropriate location
permissions, and apps targeting Android 14 or later must declare the correct foreground-
service type for a location foreground service.
Important Expo limitation
Expo supports background location through its Location and TaskManager APIs, but
background updates remain subject to platform constraints. Expo states that background
location stops if the user terminates the application and resumes after the app is restarted.
Therefore, your product must detect and report:
• App terminated
• Background permission removed
• Location disabled
• Tracking task stopped
• Network unavailable
• Points pending upload
Do not falsely label these situations as a completed, continuously tracked route.

Context matters
No movement may be acceptable when:

• Pet rests
• Sitter gives water
• Traffic crossing is delayed
• Customer requested a stationary outdoor break
• GPS signal is weak
• Service is pet sitting rather than walking
Recommended rule
Use:
• No significant movement
• For a sustained period
• During a walking service
• With acceptable GPS accuracy
• Without a pause reason
First prompt the sitter:
You have been stationary for several minutes. Is everything okay?
Escalate only when the sitter fails to respond or another risk signal exists.

Product 3: AI-Assisted Sitter Matching
1. Product objective
The matching system should reduce:
• Manual search time
• Poor distance assignments
• Skill mismatches
• Schedule conflicts
• Repeated sitter changes
• Last-minute cancellations
• Subscription fulfilment risk
It should not remove human accountability.

NIST’s AI-risk guidance recommends defining where human oversight is necessary,
documenting system limitations, providing understandable outputs and continuously
monitoring performance and harmful outcomes. That is especially relevant here because
matching affects both pet safety and sitter earning opportunities.
2. Why full auto-assignment is premature
A pet-care assignment contains context that may not be completely represented in
structured data:
• The dog recently became reactive
• The customer distrusts a particular replacement
• A society gate has changed its rules
• A sitter has accepted too many consecutive walks
• A medical or behavioural note is ambiguous
• A location appears close geographically but is difficult to reach
• The sitter is technically available but is the only backup for another subscription
An automated system may produce a mathematically plausible match that is operationally
unsafe.
Recommended responsibility
Actor Responsibility
System Filters ineligible sitters
Ranking engine Orders eligible candidates
Admin Reviews context and confirms
Sitter Accepts the assignment
Customer Confirms where appropriate
Quality team Audits results and failures
3. Three-stage matching architecture
Stage 1: Hard eligibility filters
Before any AI scoring, eliminate sitters who do not satisfy mandatory conditions.

Hard filters
• Sitter account is active
• Required documents are current
• Correct service permission exists
• Correct city and service zone
• Available at requested time
• Travel time is feasible
• Daily capacity is available
• Pet-risk level is permitted
• Sitter has required skills
• Society access is valid
• No overlapping booking
• Sitter is not paused or under investigation
• Required backup coverage remains available
All sitters
↓
Hard safety and operational rules
↓
Eligible candidate pool
The AI should never “outscore” a failed safety rule.
Stage 2: Candidate ranking
Rank only the eligible pool.
Recommended factors
Factor Suggested importance
Previous relationship with pet Very high
Pet-risk and skill compatibility Very high
Availability fit Very high

Factor Suggested importance
Travel time High
Reliability High
Service-specific experience High
Customer preference Medium-high
Society access familiarity Medium-high
Rating and report quality Medium
Price/payout compatibility Medium
Backup implications Medium
Example scoring model
Match score = 20%×pet compatibility
+20%×repeat relationship
+15%×reliability
+15%×travel fit
+10%×availability fit
+10%×customer preference
+5%×service quality
+5%×backup health
Weights should vary by service.
For example:
• Dog walking: distance, punctuality and previous pet relationship matter strongly.
• Boarding: environment, trial history and household compatibility matter more.
• Senior care: relevant skill and medical-instruction reliability dominate.
• Grooming: package skill, pet size and equipment matter more than distance alone.

10. Matching fairness and worker controls
Matching can affect how many earning opportunities each sitter receives. Therefore, avoid
creating a system that permanently sends all work to a small number of already successful
providers.

Track:
• Recommendations per sitter
• Assignments per sitter
• Acceptance rate
• Earnings distribution
• New-sitter exposure
• Geographic distribution
• Admin overrides
• False exclusions
• Rating bias
• Customer-preference effects
NIST recommends defining human roles, measuring errors and negative effects, monitoring
performance over time and maintaining processes to correct systems that exceed
acceptable risk levels.
New sitter cold-start policy
A new sitter cannot have:
• Past relationship history
• Many ratings
• Large completed-service volume
Create a controlled trial mechanism:
• Low-risk first assignments
• Supervised or monitored first services
• Explicit “new approved sitter” status
• No automatic penalty for limited history
• Progressive capacity increase

13. Why the “cash wallet” should be deferred
RBI defines a closed-system instrument as one used to purchase goods or services from
the issuing entity only; it cannot be used to settle third-party services and does not permit
cash withdrawal. A marketplace using independent sitters, groomers or other providers
should not automatically assume that a customer-funded wallet qualifies as an
unregulated closed system.
Therefore, avoid initially building:
• User-reloadable money balances
• Peer-to-peer transfers
• Cash withdrawal
• Transferable balances
• Payments outside your platform
• Cross-merchant acceptance
• Wallet-to-bank settlement
Before introducing those features, obtain specialist Indian payments advice regarding PPI
and marketplace-payment treatment.

Important rules
• Use a stable app-generated installation_id.
• Keep one push-token record per app installation and provider.
• Never treat a push token as an authentication credential.
• Encrypt the usable token at rest because the server must retrieve it to send
notifications.
• Do not write push tokens into application logs.
• Mark tokens invalid after permanent provider errors.
• Detach or revoke the token when a user logs out of a shared device.
Refresh tokens should use rotation: each refresh issues a new refresh token and
invalidates the previous one while retaining the token-family relationship for replay
detection. This is the current OAuth security best practice.

On the device, refresh tokens should be stored in secure platform-backed storage, such as
Expo SecureStore, rather than AsyncStorage or ordinary local files. Expo SecureStore is
intended for small secrets such as tokens and keys.

16. Security requirements
Authentication
• Rotating refresh tokens
• Short-lived access tokens
• Per-device sessions
• Session revocation
• OTP and login rate limits
• MFA for administrators
• Reauthentication for high-risk actions
• No tokens in URLs or logs
Authorization
Use RBAC plus contextual checks:
Role
+ city scope
+ service-zone scope
+ booking relationship

+ action permission
Examples:
• A sitter can read only currently assigned bookings.
• A customer can read only their own pets and bookings.
• A city manager can access only assigned cities.
• A society user can see aggregate society information.
• A vet can access only explicitly shared pet records.
PostgreSQL Row-Level Security can restrict which rows a database role may select or
modify and provides a default-deny posture when enabled without an applicable policy.
Use it as defence in depth, not as a replacement for application authorization.
Device integrity
Consider Play Integrity for high-risk Android actions such as:
• Login from a new device
• Credit adjustment attempts
• Suspicious tracking submissions
• Referral qualification
• High-value booking activity
Play Integrity allows the backend to assess whether requests originate from the genuine
app installed through Google Play on a recognized device. It should provide a risk signal—
not automatically block every unsupported device.

17. Location privacy policy
Mandatory rules
1. Track only during a sitter-initiated eligible service.
2. Stop tracking automatically when the service ends.
3. Do not track during off-duty periods.
4. Explain foreground and background use before requesting permission.
5. Show tracking status visibly to the sitter.
6. Give customers access only to their active or historical booking.
7. Restrict admin access to authorized operations and safety roles.
8. Log every sensitive administrative access.
9. Define and enforce route-data retention.

10. Delete or de-identify raw points after the retention purpose expires.
11. Retain incident-related routes separately under a documented legal or investigation
hold.
12. Do not send raw routes to general analytics tools.
Android requires developers to accurately declare location-data collection and sharing,
and background-location access is treated distinctly from ordinary foreground location.
The DPDP Act requires consent requests to be presented clearly and in plain language,
while the notified Rules establish the current implementation framework. Location notices
should therefore explain the purpose, duration, recipients, controls and grievance contact
in straightforward language.
Recommended data separation
Exact GPS points
→ restricted tracking store
Derived distance/duration
→ ordinary booking report
Service zone and city
→ operational analytics
De-identified aggregate patterns
→ capacity and route analysis
Exact customer coordinates and access codes should not be available to marketing,
finance or society roles.
18. User-facing location wording
Short permission explanation
Location during active services
Your location is collected only while you start and perform an active pet-care service. It
helps verify arrival, share live service updates, document the service route and provide
safety support. Tracking stops when the service ends.

Detailed wording
When you start an eligible pet-care service, the app may collect your location while the app
is open and, where required for route continuity, while it runs in the background. The pet
parent can view location updates only for their active booking. Authorized operations and
safety staff may access the information when needed to manage the service, investigate an
incident or provide support.
The app does not track your location outside an active service. Route data is retained only
for the period described in our privacy notice and is then deleted or de-identified unless it
is required for an open safety, support or legal matter.
Interrupted tracking message for customers
Live location is temporarily unavailable. The service remains in progress, and our
operations team has been notified.
Avoid blaming the sitter when the cause may be:
• Network loss
• Permission change
• Device shutdown
• Operating-system restriction
• GPS inaccuracy

Phase 11 Six-Month Execution Plan
Executive verdict
Approve the six-month roadmap, with five structural corrections:

1. Prototype background GPS in Month 1, rather than discovering technical
limitations in Week 9.
2. Build the admin command centre alongside the sitter app, because it must
receive and act on sitter events.
3. Replace “wallet” with an immutable service-credit ledger. Defer customer-funded
cash balances.
4. Launch rules-based, explainable matching first; advanced AI comes after
sufficient outcome data exists.
5. Security, privacy, physical-device QA and app-store preparation must run
throughout the programme—not only during Week 23.

↓
Sitter app foundation
↓
Tracking + emergency + admin operations
↓
Customer app
↓
Subscriptions + credits + referrals
↓
Matching assistance + hardening
↓
Controlled store launch
Expo background location and remote push notifications require development builds
rather than relying only on Expo Go. Expo also documents that background location stops if
the user terminates the application, so this limitation must be tested and represented
truthfully in the operational state model from the first month.

Main principle
Request a permission at the moment the user activates the related feature—not during first

Android recommends associating runtime permission requests with the specific user

Location
Sitter-app use

Risk 1: App development delays
Root causes
• Building sitter and customer apps simultaneously
• Adding AI, loyalty and health features before the core workflow works
• Discovering GPS limitations late

• Rebuilding backend logic inside the app
• Treating every feature as P0
Prevention
Use four controlled release units:
1. Sitter service-execution vertical slice
2. Admin exception-management workflow
3. Customer booking and live-status workflow
4. Retention and intelligence features
The first production-quality vertical slice should cover:
Login
→ Assigned booking
→ Arrival
→ Start service
→ GPS/session evidence
→ End service
→ Report submission
→ Admin visibility
Do not begin customer loyalty or advanced AI while this flow remains unreliable.
Leading indicators
• Increasing unfinished work each sprint
• More than 20–25% of sprint work carried forward
• Backend contracts changing after mobile development begins
• Native-location prototype still unproven after Month 1
• P0 defect count growing rather than shrinking
Risk 2: GPS battery drain and unreliable tracking
A single aggressive location interval is not appropriate for every service. Use adaptive
collection based on movement, accuracy, battery condition and service type.

Expo supports background-location tasks through development builds, but its
documentation notes that updates stop if the user terminates the app and resume when
the app is reopened. The product must represent this as an interruption rather than
showing a falsely continuous route.

Battery monitoring Test real devices and OEMs
Stop condition
Pause tracking rollout when:
• Tracking continues after service completion
• Battery or thermal issues materially affect devices
• More than 5% of eligible sessions fail without a recovery path
• Location points are silently lost
• Staff cannot distinguish network loss from deliberate tracking disablement
Risk 3: Privacy concerns
The official rule must be:
Location is collected only during an explicitly started active pet-care service and is
stopped when that service ends.
Google Play requires background-location access to support an important core feature,
accompanied by prominent in-app disclosure, a privacy policy and an accurate
permissions declaration. Apple also requires location collection to be directly relevant to
app functionality and accurately disclosed.

The Indian DPDP framework requires digital personal data to be processed for lawful
purposes with clear notices and appropriate safeguards. The 2025 Rules use phased
commencement, so product controls should be built before wider enforcement and scale.
Mandatory safeguards
• No off-duty or between-booking tracking
• Visible tracking indicator
• Customer access only to their booking
• Admin access limited to operations and safety roles
• Access audit history
• Defined raw-route retention
• Incident-related legal hold handled separately
• Raw routes excluded from ordinary analytics
• Sitter can see permission and tracking status
• Privacy notice states purpose, access and retention
Approved user-facing wording
Location during active services
Your location is collected only while you perform an eligible pet-care service. It helps verify
arrival, provide service updates, document the route and support safety assistance.
Tracking stops when the service is completed.
Risk 4: Bugs during real bookings
A mobile defect can cause more than inconvenience. It can affect pet custody, customer
access, payment, provider earnings and incident handling.
Required protections
Internal alpha
→ Sitter closed beta
→ Customer closed beta
→ One-cluster production
→ One-city production
→ Multi-city rollout
Use independent feature flags for:

• Mobile booking
• GPS
• Route sharing
• Credit payments
• AI recommendations
• Emergency workflows
• City and service-zone availability
Keep the PWA operational as a fallback.
Apple TestFlight supports up to 100 internal testers and up to 10,000 external testers.
Google recommends moving from internal testing to a controlled closed test; certain newer
personal Play developer accounts must complete a closed test with at least 12 testers
opted in for 14 continuous days before applying for production access.
Release blockers

• Cross-customer access
• Incorrect credit consumption

• Unrecoverable offline report

Risk 8: Wallet and credit disputes
The early product should be called Credits, not Wallet.
Use:
• Subscription service credits
• Referral credits
• Promotional credits
• Society benefits
• Service-recovery credits
Do not initially support:

• Customer-funded cash storage
• Transfers between users
• Cash withdrawal
• Open merchant usage
RBI distinguishes closed-system instruments used only for the issuer’s own services from
broader prepaid instruments, and closed systems cannot be used for third-party
settlement or cash withdrawal. A marketplace with independent providers should obtain
specialist payments advice before introducing a cash-like stored-value product.
Ledger requirements
Every credit movement must be append-only:
GRANT
RESERVE
CONSUME
RELEASE
RESTORE
EXPIRE
REVERSE
ADMIN_ADJUSTMENT
Every transaction needs:
• Idempotency key
• Reason
• Source booking/subscription
• Actor
• Expiry
• Timestamp
• Reversal link where applicable
Risk 9: App-store rejection
Store preparation should start while the apps are being built—not in the final week.
Common rejection areas

• Background location lacks a core use case
• Permission disclosure is vague
• Screenshots show unavailable features
• Demo account fails
• Privacy policy does not match actual SDK behaviour
• Account deletion is missing
• App crashes or has incomplete flows
• Data Safety or App Privacy declarations are inaccurate
Apple requires apps supporting account creation to let users initiate account deletion
inside the app. Google Play requires an in-app deletion path and an external web resource
for account-deletion requests.
Apple requires developers to disclose data collected by the application and integrated
third-party partners. Google Play similarly requires accurate Data Safety declarations and
may take enforcement action when app behaviour conflicts with the declaration.
Risk 10: Push notifications are treated as guaranteed delivery
Push is useful but should not be the only operational channel.
Firebase recommends storing token timestamps, refreshing tokens and removing stale or
invalid registrations.
For critical events use:
Backend event
+ in-app inbox
+ push
+ operations queue
+ SMS/call fallback where necessary
Do not define “push reliability” only as messages submitted to FCM or APNs.
Measure:
• Active-token coverage
• Provider acceptance
• Application receipt where measurable

• User acknowledgement
• Fallback activation
• Stale-token rate

6. Final Phase 11 recommendation
Build:
A sitter-first mobile operating system connected to an advanced command centre,
followed by a customer application for repeated booking, live service visibility,
subscriptions, credits and preferred-caregiver continuity.
Do
• Build sitter execution first.
• Use React Native with Expo development builds.
• Validate GPS on real Android and iOS devices early.
• Keep AI recommendations explainable and admin-approved.
• Use an immutable service-credit ledger.
• Launch through controlled cohorts.
• Keep the PWA operational.
• Maintain kill switches and rollback controls.
• Treat security and privacy testing as continuous engineering work.
Do not
• Track sitters outside active services.

• Build a cash-like wallet without regulatory analysis.
• auto-assign high-risk bookings.
• depend on push alone for emergency communication.
• expose exact customer data before assignment.
• publish both apps to every city simultaneously.
• add social, insurance or e-commerce distractions.
• call app downloads the primary success metric.
